source.title: Precise Statistical Analysis of Classification Accuracies for Adversarial Training

record.file_problem: None noted; the full paper is present, although some equations show text-extraction artifacts.
record.tranche_reason: The paper reports its own model-complexity sweeps and explicitly says it does not observe double descent in the tested linear-classification setting.
record.gate_note: The paper also reports accuracy curves versus adversary power and compares theory with simulations; those results do not measure the claim versions. Results cited from other studies are not recorded as rows.
record.test_reason: The paper sweeps d/n (which it calls model complexity) for adversarially trained and standard (ε0=0) linear classifiers on a Gaussian mixture. It reports test standard accuracy across the separability (interpolation) threshold and states that no double descent appears. This is a new-setting result on V3 and V4 rather than a dedicated refutation, so T3 fits better than T5.
record.authors_conclusion: Mostly correct. The authors report that, for their setting, standard accuracy always decreases as d/n grows (at different rates in the separable and non-separable regimes), with no double descent. They explicitly contrast this with prior double-descent findings, and note that double descent has been seen for binary linear classification under model misspecification [DKT19], which they do not analyse.
record.recipe_differences: The study analyzes robust minimax adversarial training of linear classifiers on Gaussian-mixture data, rather than deep-network size sweeps.
record.method_sensitivity: The reported curves depend on perturbation norm (ℓ2 versus ℓ∞), adversary power ε0, and whether the setting is separable or non-separable.

fits_no_version.finding: Robust accuracy vs d/n (Figs 4b, 6b) also declines with complexity; LDA vs minimax robust accuracy vs 1/δ (Figs 9b, 10b).
fits_no_version.proposed_claim: Robust (adversarial) test accuracy of adversarially trained linear classifiers degrades monotonically with overparameterization d/n.

record.problems: Evidence for the complexity trends is presented as curves; exact values and uncertainty intervals are not stated in the text. The results concern theoretical predictions and simulations for a particular linear-classification data model, not deep networks or a broad set of model classes.

untested.parts: No deep networks; linear classifiers only.
No test error across training epochs.
No effective-complexity measure predicting peak location.
No label noise, no multiple peaks, no tuned-regularization comparison. ε0 acts like a regularizer, but there is no peak for it to remove.
Only the well-specified Gaussian-mixture linear classifier. The misspecified setting where DKT19 found double descent is explicitly not analysed.
Only linear classifiers on an isotropic GMM where added dimensions carry no extra signal (||µ|| fixed). No random features, kernels or trees.

missing.what: Whether Fig 4/6 complexity curves include empirical simulation dots or are purely asymptotic theory is not stated; matters for weighing the evidence.
missing.locator: Figures 4 and 6 captions ('similar setting as in Figure 3')

record.verdict_notes: Rows were relabelled from reversed to absent: monotone error is no second descent, not an opposite effect. Labels were set to limits_scope rather than challenges because the result concerns one well-specified linear setting. In that setting, extra dimensions add only noise (||µ|| fixed), unlike the feature-addition settings where double descent is reported, and the authors themselves point to a misspecified variant that does show it.

versions.untested_parts: The paper studies linear classifiers, not deep-network model-size sweeps.
It does not report test error across training epochs.
The sample-size trend is tested in the paper's specified linear-classification and adversarial-training settings, not generally across model classes or data settings.
The reported test is limited to the paper's linear-classification setting and its specified adversarial-training experiments.
No single effective-complexity measure is tested as predicting peak locations across size, epochs, and samples.
The paper does not test label-noise-driven peaks, multiple descent, or optimally tuned regularization removing the peak.
It does not compare descent curves under an alternative effective-parameter count.

rows.subject: robust minimax linear classifier (θ̂ε; max-margin classifier in the separable regime)
rows.operation_detail: Sweep dimension-to-sample ratio 1/δ, with p = 2 perturbations.
rows.measure: Standard accuracy on unperturbed test data
rows.note: The text says standard accuracy decreases as 1/δ grows, including across the separable and non-separable regimes; the figure plots several ε0 curves.
rows.check: State should be absent, not reversed. The text says SA always decreases as 1/δ grows, so there is no second descent past the separability threshold and no sample-wise rise. Monotone error is the absence of the version's effect, not its opposite. Values are figure-only, and the curves are mainly asymptotic theory (d=400 setting inherited from Fig 3). This ε0=0 curve is the non-adversarial max-margin case, the most direct test.

relationships.condition: Well-specified isotropic Gaussian-mixture linear classifiers, ℓ2 and ℓ∞ adversarial training, ε0 ∈ {0, 0.3, 0.7, 1} (including the non-adversarial max-margin case ε0=0)
relationships.reason: SA decreases monotonically in d/n across the separability threshold with no second descent (r1–r8). The authors note double descent does appear in this model class under feature misspecification [DKT19], so the result qualifies the generality of V4 rather than refuting it. Evidence is figure-only.
relationships.display_finding: Standard accuracy decreased monotonically with d/n across the separability threshold, without renewed risk improvement.
